title: Is In-Context Reinforcement Learning A Posterior Sampler? An Empirical Study

paper.title: Is In-Context Reinforcement Learning A Posterior Sampler? An Empirical Study
paper.abstract: Abstract In-context reinforcement learning (ICRL) exploits the impressive in-context learning ability of large language models to zero-shot generalize to new, unseen tasks at inference time without any parameter updates. Among many approaches, the Decision-Pretrained Transformer (DPT) is particularly appealing for its theoretical grounding: under idealized assumptions such as a sufficiently expressive model and infinite pretraining data, DPT can perform Bayesian posterior sampling. Whether this characterization survives in practice remains open. Therefore, we ask: is ICRL, specifically DPT and our proposed DPT variants, a Bayesian posterior sampler in practice? To approach this question, we establish two necessary conditions that a Bayesian posterior sampler must satisfy: sufficient-statistic invariance and the martingale property . We then construct statistical hypothesis tests to statistically assess if practically-trained ICRL models satisfy these conditions. Applying these tests in Gaussian, Bernoulli, and linear bandit settings, we find that both conditions are consistently violated, suggesting that ICRL may not behave as Bayesian posterior samplers in practice. Beyond this negative result, our tests provide a principled toolkit for testing the Bayesian behavior of ICRL.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated remarkable performance in a wide range of applications, such as strategy games ( Mnih et al., 2013 ; Mnih et al., 2015 ) , robotics ( Levine et al., 2016 ; Duan et al., 2016 ) , and recommender systems ( Afsar et al., 2023 ; Lin et al., 2024b ) . However, a fundamental challenge in RL is the limited capability to few-shot or zero-shot generalize to new unseen tasks, as traditional RL methods learn a policy for a single task through an ocean of environment interactions and extensive trials-and-errors, and thus typically requires retraining a policy from scratch for each new task. In-context RL (ICRL) offers a compelling alternative attributed to the impressive capability of in-context learning by large language models (LLMs) ( Dong et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Wei et al., 2023 ) . Specifically, a transformer ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) pretrained on a diverse set of tasks/environments can adapt to and reinforcement learn in new, unseen tasks at test time, purely by conditioning on interactions with the new, unseen tasks (a.k.a. context) without any parameter updates. Several ICRL frameworks have been proposed to realize this vision. Algorithm Distillation (AD) pretrains a transformer on the complete learning histories of an RL algorithm (e.g., PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) or SAC ( Haarnoja et al., 2018 ) ), where the context consists of a sequence of episodes exhibiting progressive improvement and dynamics ( Laskin et al., 2023 ) . The transformer learns to extrapolate this improvement operator, effectively distilling the source RL algorithm’s learning dynamics into its in-context behavior. Decision-Pretrained Transformer (DPT) adopts a fundamentally different approach ( Lee et al., 2023 ) . Rather than imitating an evolving algorithm, DPT pretrains a transformer via supervised learning to predict optimal actions conditioned on contexts of varying lengths. Moreover, DPT can employ arbitrary context data, such as interactions collected under a random policy ( Chen and Paternain, 2025 ) , by leveraging the optimal action labels. Notably, a central theoretical grounding underpins DPT’s appeal. Prior works ( Lee et al., 2023 ; Lin et al., 2024a ) establish a theoretical understanding that “DPT is an efficient implementation of Bayesian posterior sampling ” that achieves rate-optimal Bayesian regret ( Russo and Van Roy, 2016 ) . This, however, relies on strong assumptions such as a sufficiently expressive model and infinite pretraining data to exactly match or closely approximate the pretraining data distribution ( Lee et al., 2023 ; Lin et al., 2024a ) , which may not hold in practice. (a) Cumulative regret (b) TV distance Figure 1: DPT versus Thompson Sampling in Gaussian bandits: cumulative regret and total variation (TV) distance between action distributions. In addition, an empirical gap between DPT and a Bayesian posterior sampler (PS) is observed from experiments (see Figure 1 ), where we compare the default setting of DPT as in ( Lee et al., 2023 ) and Thompson sampling ( Thompson, 1933 ) (a Bayesian posterior sampler in multi-armed bandits) in Gaussian (multi-armed) bandits. Accordingly, this paper aims to explore and answer the following research question: Is ICRL, including DPT and our proposed DPT variants, a Bayesian posterior sampler in practice? Furthermore, it is worth highlighting that the research question above is also motivated by an empirical study ( Falck et al., 2024 ) , where in-context learning of common LLMs like GPT-3.5 ( OpenAI, n.d. ) , GPT-4 ( OpenAI, 2023 ) , Llama-2 ( Touvron et al., 2023 ) , and Mistral ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) is demonstrated non-Bayesian from a martingale perspective (a necessary condition for Bayesian systems). Inspired by ( Falck et al., 2024 ) , we take a statistical hypothesis testing approach to the research question above. Our main contributions are as follows. • Necessary conditions. We provide a behavioral characterization of a transformer as a Bayesian posterior sampler in terms of its action distribution, and derive two necessary conditions from it, namely sufficient-statistic invariance and the martingale property , which we instantiate for Gaussian, Bernoulli, and linear bandits. • Testing framework and DPT variants. We turn each condition into a hypothesis test on action probabilities. Since DPT predicts only actions, we propose DPT ′ and GDPT, which augment DPT with a reward head so that the martingale property becomes testable. • Empirical findings. Across all bandit settings, deployment modes, context transformations, and context lengths, DPT, DPT ′ , and GDPT consistently violate sufficient-statistic invariance, and DPT ′ and GDPT additionally violate the martingale property, even when their decision performance closely tracks Thompson Sampling. Ablation studies that enforce permutation invariance do not remove the violations. Beyond this negative result, our statistical tests provide a principled toolkit for auditing Bayesian claims about ICRL. A more detailed discussion of related work is provided in Appendix A .

sections.heading: 3 Are DPT and Its Variants Bayesian Posterior Samplers?
sections.text: Having introduced the DPT framework, we emphasize that the idealized assumptions under which DPT is expected to behave as a Bayesian posterior sampler, such as a sufficiently expressive model and infinite pretraining data, may not hold in practice. To investigate whether DPT exhibits Bayesian posterior sampling behavior in practice, this section establishes two necessary conditions that any Bayesian posterior sampler must satisfy and develops a statistical testing framework to quantitatively assess if DPT and its variants satisfies these conditions. All proofs in this section are provided in Appendix B.1 . We begin by characterizing the transformer as a Bayesian posterior sampler, motivated by its role as the common decision-making component across most ICRL algorithms, including DPT.

sections.heading: 3.1 Transformer as a Bayesian Posterior Sampler

sections.heading: 3.2 DPT Variants
sections.text: The two proposed DPT variants, DPT ′ and GDPT, retain DPT’s transformer backbone and incorporate an additional reward head to jointly predict actions and their associated rewards. DPT ′ and GDPT differ only in their supervision labels, as described below. DPT ′ . This variant is identical to DPT except that it extends DPT’s optimal action prediction to a joint prediction of the optimal action and its associated reward. The training objective for DPT ′ is the cross-entropy loss for both the action head and the reward head. GDPT. This variant employs the same architecture as DPT ′ . However, rather than predicting the optimal action and its associated reward as in DPT ′ , GDPT is trained to autoregressively predict the next action-reward pair in the context. Consequently, GDPT does not require optimal actions and rewards as supervision labels. This is similar to the training procedure of AD ( Laskin et al., 2023 ) , which, however, lacks a reward head and predicts only actions. On the other hand, GDPT requires expert contexts for training (same as AD), such as Thompson sampling trajectories, whereas DPT and DPT ′ can be trained on arbitrary contexts, including both random and expert contexts ( Lee et al., 2023 ) . This distinction arises from the availability of optimal supervision labels for DPT and DPT ′ . It is worth noting that both DPT ′ and GDPT satisfy the conditions of Proposition 1 by construction. Specifically, both variants employ Gaussian reward heads whose structures mirror those of the action heads, which are supposed to be context-independent under Definition 1 . Moreover, given a context, both DPT ′ and GDPT can generate future continuations according to their respective posterior-predictive distributions, as required by Proposition 2 .

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: This section presents experimental results for the two statistical tests developed in Section 3.3 . We first describe the shared experimental setup, then present results for DPT, DPT ′ , and GDPT in Gaussian, Bernoulli, and linear bandits settings. Following these, we investigate the effect of the transformer’s architecture through an ablation study.

sections.heading: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Environments (Tasks). We consider three bandit problems: Gaussian, Bernoulli, and linear bandits. In Gaussian bandits, rewards satisfy r | a ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ a , σ 2 ) r\mid a\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{a},\sigma^{2}) with unknown arm means { μ a } \{\mu_{a}\} and known variance σ 2 \sigma^{2} . In Bernoulli bandits, rewards satisfy r | a ∼ Bernoulli ⁡ ( p a ) r\mid a\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_{a}) with unknown success probabilities { p a } \{p_{a}\} . In linear bandits, each arm a a is associated with a fixed, known feature vector x a ∈ ℝ d x_{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , and rewards satisfy r | a ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( x a ⊤ ​ θ , σ 2 ) r\mid a\sim\mathcal{N}(x_{a}^{\top}\theta,\sigma^{2}) with an unknown shared parameter θ ∈ ℝ d \theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and known variance σ 2 \sigma^{2} . Gaussian and Bernoulli bandits can be viewed as special cases of linear bandits. Pretraining and Deployment. The dataset collection, pretraining, and deployment procedures for DPT, DPT ′ , and GDPT follow Section 2 . For online deployment, the contexts are collected by the model itself. For offline deployment, the contexts are pre-specified by either a Dirichlet-mixture random policy or Thompson Sampling depending on the bandit setting, following ( Lee et al., 2023 ) . Tests and Metrics. Under Proposition 1 , a Bayesian posterior sampler with the assumed reward likelihood must be invariant to transformations preserving the sufficient statistic. For a context D n D_{n} , let N a N_{a} and S a S_{a} be the number of pulls and the total rewards of arm a a . The sufficient statistic is { ( N a , S a ) } a = 1 K \{(N_{a},S_{a})\}_{a=1}^{K} for Gaussian and Bernoulli bandits, and ( V = ∑ a N a ​ x a ​ x a ⊤ , b = ∑ a x a ​ S a ) \big(V=\sum_{a}N_{a}x_{a}x_{a}^{\top},b=\sum_{a}x_{a}S_{a}\big) for linear bandits (details in Appendix B.3 ). We test this invariance with two transformations: sorting reorders the action-reward pairs in ascending order of reward, reward replacement replaces each arm’s rewards with its empirical mean plus centered uniform noise. Since Bernoulli rewards only take values in { 0 , 1 } \{0,1\} , we only use sorting . Each test evaluates the hypothesis in Eq. ( 10 ) on N = 5000 N=5000 independently sampled environments and their contexts. For the martingale test, we fix one starting context D n D_{n} , generate independent continuations of length m m using the model’s own future action and reward predictions, and test Eq. ( 12 ). Both tests are carried out with the paired Hotelling tests with significance level α = 0.05 \alpha=0.05 (see Appendix C.1 ). In addition, we compare cumulative regret, offline suboptimality, and the total variation (TV) distance of action distributions against Thompson Sampling, a canonical posterior sampling method. Hyperparameters. Appendix C.2 provides a complete list of the hyperparameters used in our experiments, including those specifying the transformer’s architecture and the experimental setup.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we investigate whether ICRL, specifically DPT and two variants DPT ′ and GDPT, behave as Bayesian posterior samplers in practice, where the idealized assumptions underpinning its theoretical characterization may not hold. We establish two necessary conditions that any Bayesian posterior sampler must satisfy: sufficient-statistic invariance and the martingale property. Then we design statistical hypothesis tests for both conditions. Experiments on Gaussian, Bernoulli, and linear bandits show that DPT, DPT ′ , and GDPT consistently violate the sufficient-statistic invariance. Additionally, DPT ′ and GDPT violate the martingale property under their own model-generated continuations, even when their decision performance is comparable to that of Thompson Sampling. The ablation study further exhibits that enforcing permutation invariance in the architecture restores invariance to the context order but recovers neither condition, indicating that the sensitivity to the context order is not the main source of these violations. Beyond these negative findings, our tests rely only on observable action predictions and thus provide a principled toolkit for examining Bayesian claims about ICRL. Extending the tests to decision-making problems with state dependence, and understanding what architectural and training choices are needed to satisfy the two conditions, are important directions for future work.

sections.heading: In-context reinforcement learning.
sections.text: Transformers have been successfully applied to RL by formulating decision-making as a sequence modeling problem. Two pioneering works, Decision Transformer and Trajectory Transformer, take different approaches. Decision Transformer predicts actions conditioned on desired returns and past interactions ( Chen et al., 2021 ) , while Trajectory Transformer models trajectories autoregressively and performs planning via beam search ( Janner et al., 2021 ) . In-context reinforcement learning (ICRL) takes this paradigm a step further by studying how pretrained transformers can adapt to new, unseen tasks without any parameter updates. Laskin et al. (2023) introduced Algorithm Distillation (AD), which pretrains a causal transformer on the learning histories generated by a source RL algorithm, with the goal of distilling its policy improvement operator across episodes. Lee et al. (2023) subsequently proposed the Decision-Pretrained Transformer (DPT), which predicts optimal actions given a query state and arbitrary contexts of varying lengths. DPT typically relies on optimal policies, such as well-trained PPO policies or human-designed policies, to provide supervision labels. A central theoretical grounding for DPT is that, under idealized assumptions such as a sufficiently expressive model and infinite pretraining data, it behaves as a Bayesian posterior sampler. Building on this perspective, we investigate whether DPT and our proposed DPT variants satisfy necessary conditions for the Bayesian posterior sampler in practice.

sections.heading: Is in-context learning Bayesian?
sections.text: A prominent line of work examines whether in-context learning (ICL) can be characterized as Bayesian inference. Xie et al. (2022) model pretraining data as a mixture of hidden Markov models indexed by a latent concept and demonstrate that the pretrained predictor implicitly infers the concept shared across the prompt, becoming asymptotically Bayes-optimal as the number of in-context examples grows. Wakayama and Suzuki (2025) provide a finite-sample counterpart for meta-learning over a mixture of tasks. They decompose the ICL risk into a Bayes gap and an irreducible posterior variance, and bound the former non-asymptotically for uniform-attention transformers trained by empirical risk minimization. These results establish Bayes-optimality under idealized generative assumptions, while whether trained models actually behave in a Bayesian manner remains an empirical question. Falck et al. (2024) address it by observing that Bayesian predictive distributions over exchangeable data must satisfy a martingale property, and derive testable diagnostics from it. Applied to pretrained LLMs on synthetic tasks, these diagnostics reveal systematic violations. Following this diagnostic perspective, this work statistically tests whether ICRL behaves as a Bayesian posterior sampler.

sections.heading: Bayesian posterior sampling in decision-making.
sections.text: Bayesian posterior sampling, originating with ( Thompson, 1933 ) , selects actions by drawing an environment from the current posterior and acting optimally for that draw. Russo and Van Roy (2016) give an information-theoretic analysis of Thompson sampling, bounding Bayesian regret through the information ratio, which trades off instantaneous regret against information gained about the optimal action, and obtaining regret bounds for finite-armed and linear bandits. Osband et al. (2013) extend posterior sampling to episodic Markov decision processes (MDPs) with Bayesian regret guarantees, which samples an MDP from the posterior at the start of each episode and following its optimal policy. These works characterize the exact posterior sampling, whereas this paper explores whether ICRL schemes can be viewed as posterior samplers in practice.

An Empirical Study Weiqin Chen † † thanks: Equal contribution Xinlong Du * Gesualdo Scutari Harsha Honnappa Affiliation: Edwardson School of Industrial Engineering, Purdue University Affiliation: West Lafayette, IN 47907, USA Affiliation: {chen6439, du339, gscutari, honnappa}@purdue.edu Abstract In-context reinforcement learning (ICRL) exploits the impressive in-context learning ability of large language models to zero-shot generalize to new, unseen tasks at inference time without any parameter updates. Among many approaches, the Decision-Pretrained Transformer (DPT) is particularly appealing for its theoretical grounding: under idealized assumptions such as a sufficiently expressive model and infinite pretraining data, DPT can perform Bayesian posterior sampling. Whether this characterization survives in practice remains open. Therefore, we ask: is ICRL, specifically DPT and our proposed DPT variants, a Bayesian posterior sampler in practice? To approach this question, we establish two necessary conditions that a Bayesian posterior sampler must satisfy: sufficient-statistic invariance and the martingale property . We then construct statistical hypothesis tests to statistically assess if practically-trained ICRL models satisfy these conditions. Applying these tests in Gaussian, Bernoulli, and linear bandit settings, we find that both conditions are consistently violated, suggesting that ICRL may not behave as Bayesian posterior samplers in practice. Beyond this negative result, our tests provide a principled toolkit for testing the Bayesian behavior of ICRL. 1 Introduction Reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated remarkable performance in a wide range of applications, such as strategy games ( Mnih et al., 2013 ; Mnih et al., 2015 ) , robotics ( Levine et al., 2016 ; Duan et al., 2016 ) , and recommender systems ( Afsar et al., 2023 ; Lin et al., 2024b ) . However, a fundamental challenge in RL is the limited capability to few-shot or zero-shot generalize to new unseen tasks, as traditional RL methods learn a policy for a single task through an ocean of environment interactions and extensive trials-and-errors, and thus typically requires retraining a policy from scratch for each new task. In-context RL (ICRL) offers a compelling alternative attributed to the impressive capability of in-context learning by large language models (LLMs) ( Dong et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Wei et al., 2023 ) . Specifically, a transformer ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) pretrained on a diverse set of tasks/environments can adapt to and reinforcement learn in new, unseen tasks at test time, purely by conditioning on interactions with the new, unseen tasks (a.k.a. context) without any parameter updates. Several ICRL frameworks have been proposed to realize this vision. Algorithm Distillation (AD) pretrains a transformer on the complete learning histories of an RL algorithm (e.g., PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) or SAC ( Haarnoja et al., 2018 ) ), where the context consists of a sequence of episodes exhibiting progressive improvement and dynamics ( Laskin et al., 2023 ) . The transformer learns to extrapolate this improvement operator, effectively distilling the source RL algorithm’s learning dynamics into its in-context behavior. Decision-Pretrained Transformer (DPT) adopts a fundamentally different approach ( Lee et al., 2023 ) . Rather than imitating an evolving algorithm, DPT pretrains a transformer via supervised learning to predict optimal actions conditioned on contexts of varying lengths. Moreover, DPT can employ arbitrary context data, such as interactions collected under a random policy ( Chen and Paternain, 2025 ) , by leveraging the optimal action labels. Notably, a central theoretical grounding underpins DPT’s appeal. Prior works ( Lee et al., 2023 ; Lin et al., 2024a ) establish a theoretical understanding that “DPT is an efficient implementation of Bayesian posterior sampling ” that achieves rate-optimal Bayesian regret ( Russo and Van Roy, 2016 ) . This, however, relies on strong assumptions such as a sufficiently expressive model and infinite pretraining data to exactly match or closely approximate the pretraining data distribution ( Lee et al., 2023 ; Lin et al., 2024a ) , which may not hold in practice. (a) Cumulative regret (b) TV distance Figure 1: DPT versus Thompson Sampling in Gaussian bandits: cumulative regret and total variation (TV) distance between action distributions. In addition, an empirical gap between DPT and a Bayesian posterior sampler (PS) is observed from experiments (see Figure 1 ), where we compare the default setting of DPT as in ( Lee et al., 2023 ) and Thompson sampling ( Thompson, 1933 ) (a Bayesian posterior sampler in multi-armed bandits) in Gaussian (multi-armed) bandits. Accordingly, this paper aims to explore and answer the following research question: Is ICRL, including DPT and our proposed DPT variants, a Bayesian posterior sampler in practice? Furthermore, it is worth highlighting that the research question above is also motivated by an empirical study ( Falck et al., 2024 ) , where in-context learning of common LLMs like GPT-3.5 ( OpenAI, n.d. ) , GPT-4 ( OpenAI, 2023 ) , Llama-2 ( Touvron et al., 2023 ) , and Mistral ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) is demonstrated non-Bayesian from a martingale perspective (a necessary condition for Bayesian systems). Inspired by ( Falck et al., 2024 ) , we take a statistical hypothesis testing approach to the research question above. Our main contributions are as follows. • Necessary conditions. We provide a behavioral characterization of a transformer as a Bayesian posterior sampler in terms of its action distribution, and derive two necessary conditions from it, namely sufficient-statistic invariance and the martingale property , which we instantiate for Gaussian, Bernoulli, and linear bandits. • Testing framework and DPT variants. We turn each condition into a hypothesis test on action probabilities. Since DPT predicts only actions, we propose DPT ′ and GDPT, which augment DPT with a reward head so that the martingale property becomes testable. • Empirical findings. Across all bandit settings, deployment modes, context transformations, and context lengths, DPT, DPT ′ , and GDPT consistently violate sufficient-statistic invariance, and DPT ′ and GDPT additionally violate the martingale property, even when their decision performance closely tracks Thompson Sampling. Ablation studies that enforce permutation invariance do not remove the violations. Beyond this negative result, our statistical tests provide a principled toolkit for auditing Bayesian claims about ICRL. To address this limitation, we introduce two DPT variants in the next subsection that satisfy the conditions of Proposition 1 by construction and can generate future continuations according to their own Bayesian posterior-predictive distributions. 3.2 DPT Variants The two proposed DPT variants, DPT ′ and GDPT, retain DPT’s transformer backbone and incorporate an additional reward head to jointly predict actions and their associated rewards. DPT ′ and GDPT differ only in their supervision labels, as described below. DPT ′ . This variant is identical to DPT except that it extends DPT’s optimal action prediction to a joint prediction of the optimal action and its associated reward. The training objective for DPT ′ is the cross-entropy loss for both the action head and the reward head. GDPT. This variant employs the same architecture as DPT ′ . However, rather than predicting the optimal action and its associated reward as in DPT ′ , GDPT is trained to autoregressively predict the next action-reward pair in the context. Consequently, GDPT does not require optimal actions and rewards as supervision labels. This is similar to the training procedure of AD ( Laskin et al., 2023 ) , which, however, lacks a reward head and predicts only actions. On the other hand, GDPT requires expert contexts for training (same as AD), such as Thompson sampling trajectories, whereas DPT and DPT ′ can be trained on arbitrary contexts, including both random and expert contexts ( Lee et al., 2023 ) . This distinction arises from the availability of optimal supervision labels for DPT and DPT ′ . It is worth noting that both DPT ′ and GDPT satisfy the conditions of Proposition 1 by construction. Specifically, both variants employ Gaussian reward heads whose structures mirror those of the action heads, which are supposed to be context-independent under Definition 1 .
